one_line_idea: A page is internally consistent in hand and typeface, so per-page unsupervised adaptation (estimating one style code per page and conditioning the decoder) should beat both global models and per-glyph adaptation on historical text.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Historical OCR error concentrates in rare typefaces and idiosyncratic hands; each page, however, is usually set in a single face or written by one hand, a strong structural prior that page-agnostic models ignore.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Recognition error on hard typefaces is largely a style-mismatch problem, not a legibility problem: inferring a low-dimensional style code from a page's unlabeled glyph population and conditioning recognition on it recovers most of the rare-typeface deficit, because within-page glyph consistency makes the style identifiable without labels; this is a document-native structural prior (one page, one style), distinct from generic test-time adaptation which updates weights per sample without an identifiability argument.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Page-level style conditioning will cut CER on rare-typeface pages by at least 25% relative while changing common-typeface CER by under 2% relative, and the gain will scale with page length (more glyphs, better style identification); kill the idea if rare-typeface gains are under 8% relative or show no page-length dependence, which would falsify the identifiability mechanism.
why_important: Digitization of pre-1900 print is bottlenecked by typeface diversity; a labels-free per-page mechanism with a testable identifiability signature would be adopted immediately by heritage OCR pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Font adaptation and writer adaptation have long histories; the page-as-identifiable-style-unit framing with a page-length scaling falsification appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a style-code encoder over page glyph populations on public historical corpora, condition a recognizer on it, and evaluate CER stratified by typeface rarity and page length against unconditioned and per-glyph-adapted baselines.
main_risk: Multi-face pages (emphasis, marginalia) violate the one-style assumption and need a mixture extension that weakens the clean story.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Rare-typeface failure is treated as a data-coverage problem to be solved by synthetic font rendering at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rare typefaces may fail due to genuinely ambiguous glyph shapes (long-s, ligatures) that no style conditioning can resolve without language context.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: GT4HistOCR with Calamari or TrOCR as the base recognizer; training and stratified evaluation run in about 15 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$30).

one_line_idea: Chart-understanding models rely on rendering-template priors rather than measuring geometry: re-rendering identical data with unusual axis scales and styles collapses extraction accuracy in a way that quantifies template reliance versus true visual measurement.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A controlled re-rendering test (same underlying data, systematically varied axis transforms and styles) will reveal that extraction accuracy is dominated by style familiarity: performance on default-style renders will exceed performance on unusual-but-legible renders by a large margin, and errors will follow template predictions (e.g., reading log scales as linear) rather than random noise.

why_important: Chart QA is entering scientific-assistant pipelines where log axes are common; a template-reliance quantification with signature analysis tells us whether these systems measure or memorize.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Robustness studies exist for natural images; a data-held-fixed re-rendering protocol for charts with error-signature analysis appears missing.

one_line_idea: Repeated photocopying acts as an iterated contraction on glyph shapes with predictable attractors, so augmenting OCR training with physically iterated copy-degradation beats single-pass noise models for multi-generation documents.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Archives and legal discovery are full of Nth-generation photocopies; each copy pass applies blur, thresholding, and gain nonlinearity, and the composition of many passes produces characteristic artifacts (filled counters, broken thin strokes) unlike any single-pass degradation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The copy operator is approximately a fixed nonlinear map whose iteration drives glyphs toward attractor shapes (loops fill, stems merge); OCR error therefore grows with copy generation in a predictable, accelerating way, and training with iterated-operator augmentation (not stronger single-pass noise) recovers a large share of the multi-generation deficit because it exposes the model to the attractor geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] CER will grow superlinearly with simulated copy generation, and iterated-operator augmentation will outperform intensity-matched single-pass augmentation by at least 15% relative CER on 4th-generation-plus documents; kill the idea if the two augmentations tie within 5% relative, meaning composition structure carries no information beyond degradation strength.
why_important: Multi-generation copies are a large, ignored slice of real-world OCR failure (legal, governmental, archival); the iterated-operator insight is cheap to implement and tests a general principle about compositional degradations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Document degradation models exist, but treating copy iteration as a dynamical system with attractors and testing composition-structure against strength-matched noise appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a calibrated copy operator (blur, nonlinearity, threshold, resample), verify its realism against genuine multi-generation copies, then train recognizers with iterated versus strength-matched single-pass augmentation and compare CER by generation.
main_risk: Calibrating the operator to real photocopier behavior needs a few genuine copy chains; miscalibration would blunt the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Degradation is parameterized by strength, with composition assumed irrelevant once the marginal artifact statistics match.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strength-matched single-pass noise with heavy-tailed parameters may already cover the attractor artifacts, nullifying the composition claim.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: RVL-CDIP scans and IAM lines with TrOCR; operator implementation and the training comparison run in about 12 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$25).

one_line_idea: Whitespace is a first-class structural object in documents (gutters, margins, indentation carry the layout grammar), and representing detected whitespace separators as explicit tokens improves layout parsing of complex pages over ink-only detection.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Layout models detect ink regions (text blocks, figures) and infer structure from their arrangement; typographers, by contrast, design documents around whitespace, which is the actual separator signal (column gutters, paragraph indents, section gaps).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Explicitly detecting maximal whitespace separators and feeding them as tokens alongside ink regions provides the parser with the generative variable of layout, improving structure recovery most on dense multi-column and mixed layouts where ink-region adjacency is ambiguous.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Whitespace-token models will improve structure F1 by at least 3 points on dense multi-column subsets while changing simple single-column pages by under 0.5 points, and ablating only the whitespace tokens will remove at least 70% of the gain; kill the idea if gains are under 1 point on complex layouts.
why_important: Layout errors cascade into reading order and extraction; if whitespace is the load-bearing signal, the field's ink-centric detection paradigm needs inversion, which is cheap to test and adopt.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Whitespace analysis existed in classical document analysis; reviving it as explicit tokens inside modern transformer parsers with a complexity-stratified kill test appears untried.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute maximal-rectangle whitespace separators on public layout benchmarks, add them as input tokens to a layout transformer, and evaluate structure metrics stratified by layout complexity with the token-ablation control.
main_risk: Scanned skew and noise corrupt whitespace detection precisely on the degraded pages where help is needed most.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Whitespace is assumed implicit in ink-region coordinates, requiring no explicit representation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large layout models may already infer separator structure internally, making explicit tokens redundant except on tiny training sets.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: DocLayNet with LayoutLMv3; separator computation and comparison run in about 12 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$25).

one_line_idea: The born-digital-to-scan gap in document AI decomposes into measurable physical factors (geometric warp, sensor noise, illumination), and factor-wise ablation will show geometric warp dominates, redirecting augmentation effort.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Major layout corpora are built from born-digital PDF renderings, while deployment targets scans and photos; the transfer drop is documented but unattributed, so teams guess at augmentation recipes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The drop is decomposable by applying physical factors one at a time to born-digital pages (parametric page warp, sensor noise models, illumination gradients) and measuring marginal damage; warp will account for the largest share for layout tasks because it breaks the axis-aligned geometry priors learned from PDFs, while noise dominates only for recognition tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The three factors will explain at least 70% of the born-digital-to-scan layout-F1 drop, with warp alone at least 40% of it; kill the idea if the factors jointly explain under 40% (meaning the gap is driven by unmodeled content differences) or if the factor ranking flips across two independent scan test sets.
why_important: A validated decomposition converts augmentation design from folklore to allocation: teams spend effort proportional to measured factor shares, and corpus builders know what to add.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Domain gap decompositions exist in other areas; a pre-registered physical-factor accounting for the document born-digital-to-scan gap appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply calibrated single-factor corruptions to born-digital benchmark pages, measure per-factor layout-metric damage, fit an additive attribution against the real scan gap on two scan sets, and check ranking stability.
main_risk: Factors interact (warp changes how illumination gradients land), so an additive attribution may need interaction terms to close the accounting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The scan gap is treated as an undifferentiated 'domain shift' addressed by stacking all augmentations at once.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Content differences (real scans are older documents with different layouts) may dominate, making the physical decomposition explain little.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: PubLayNet (born-digital) versus DocLayNet scans with LayoutLMv3 and DiT baselines; the factorial study runs in about 15 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$30).
